title: Dementia and Dental Care: A Guide for Families and Carers
author: Precision Dental

imageAlt: An older couple laughing together on a sofa at home
body:
Caring for someone with Alzheimer's disease or another form of dementia means managing a great deal at once, and dental care can drift down the list. It is worth keeping on it, because oral problems are a common source of distress that the person may not be able to describe, and because they are largely preventable with a steady routine.

What the Research Does and Does Not Show

You may have seen headlines linking gum disease to dementia. The picture is more measured than those headlines suggest.

A number of studies have found an association between periodontal disease and cognitive decline, and researchers have proposed possible mechanisms, including chronic inflammation and the presence of oral bacteria in brain tissue. Association, however, is not the same as cause. People with cognitive decline often find daily cleaning harder, which itself leads to gum disease, so the relationship may run in either direction, or both.

The sensible conclusion is not that treating gum disease prevents dementia. It is that gum health is worth looking after for its own sake, and that people with dementia need extra support to maintain it.

Why Oral Health Declines With Dementia

Several things change at once:

  • The sequence of brushing becomes harder to plan and carry out
  • The person may forget whether they have cleaned their teeth
  • Dry mouth is common, partly from medications used in dementia care
  • Many people with dementia have other health conditions and take several medications, so a mouth infection adds to an already heavy load on the body
  • Diet often shifts towards soft, sweet foods that are easier to eat
  • Discomfort may be expressed as agitation or refusal to eat rather than as a complaint about a tooth
  • Accepting help with something as personal as mouth care can feel intrusive

Signs of a Dental Problem in Someone Who Cannot Tell You

Watch for:

  • Refusing food, or favouring one side when chewing
  • Pulling at the face or mouth
  • New agitation, particularly at mealtimes
  • Disturbed sleep
  • Bad breath or visible swelling
  • Bleeding on the pillow or on a cloth after mouth care
  • Dentures being removed repeatedly or left out

Any of these is worth an assessment. Pain is a common and often overlooked driver of distressed behaviour in dementia.

Practical Daily Care

Build a Simple Routine

Clean at the same times each day, in the same place. Familiarity reduces resistance. Aim for twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste, but accept that once is sometimes what is achievable.

Make the Task Easier

  • Use a soft brush with a large handle, or an electric brush if it is tolerated
  • Try the hand-over-hand method, placing your hand over theirs so the movement feels shared rather than done to them
  • Break it into short steps with clear, calm instructions, one at a time
  • Stand beside or behind rather than looming in front
  • Use a smaller amount of toothpaste if foam is distressing, and a non-foaming or mild-flavoured paste if needed
  • Clean dentures daily, label them with a name, and remove them overnight

Manage Dry Mouth

Offer water regularly, use saliva substitutes if recommended, and ask us about high-fluoride toothpaste, which reduces decay risk when saliva is low.

Watch the Diet

Sweetened drinks, supplement drinks and soft sugary foods all raise decay risk, particularly with a dry mouth. Where they are needed for nutrition, offering them at mealtimes rather than continuously through the day helps.

Planning Dental Care Early

The most useful thing families can do is act early, while the person can still tolerate and consent to treatment. In the early stage, it is worth completing any necessary work, simplifying the mouth where sensible, and addressing gum health so that maintenance in later stages is as easy as possible.

This might include restoring teeth with white fillings before decay progresses, treating gum disease, reviewing whether existing dentures fit and are labelled, and in some cases deciding whether a tooth with a poor outlook is better addressed by tooth extraction now than by an emergency later.

What to Expect From Us

Appointments for a person with dementia need a different rhythm. We allow longer, schedule for the time of day when they are usually at their best, keep the waiting time short and the room calm, and let you know in advance if we are running late. We explain each step simply and put on masks and other protective equipment only when they are needed, as a room full of covered faces can be confronting. A familiar carer is welcome to stay throughout, and seeing the same dentist over time helps build trust. Please bring an up-to-date list of medications, as several commonly prescribed in dementia care have effects on the mouth.

Our approach with anxious patients applies here too: a slower pace, clear signals, and a willingness to stop and reschedule rather than push through. Where consent is involved, we work with the person and, where appropriate, with the substitute decision-maker in line with Queensland requirements.

Regular short check-up and clean visits are usually better than occasional long ones.

Early Changes Are Sometimes Noticed in the Chair

Dementia develops gradually, and a change in someone's oral care, such as a person who has always been meticulous suddenly missing large areas, or confusion about appointments, can be one of the earlier signs. If we notice a change like this, we may mention it gently so that it can be followed up with their GP.

Looking After Yourself Too

Carers are often exhausted, and mouth care can become one more battle. If a session is refused, leave it and try later rather than forcing it. Tell us what is and is not working at home, and we will adjust our advice to what is realistic rather than ideal.

Appointments in Residential Care

If the person you care for has moved into residential aged care, oral care often needs advocating for. Ask what the facility's oral care policy is, whether staff are trained to assist with brushing and denture cleaning, and how dental reviews are arranged.

It helps to provide clearly labelled dentures, a named toothbrush and toothpaste, and a short written summary of what works: the time of day they cope best, the position they accept, and any phrases that help. Reviewing the mouth yourself during visits, when you can, often picks up problems earlier than a busy roster allows.

Where attending a practice becomes difficult, discuss the options with us, including what can reasonably be simplified so that care remains manageable. Dementia Australia also provides practical resources for families and carers, including guidance on daily mouth care.

Talk to Us About Care Planning

If you are supporting someone with dementia, we are happy to discuss a plan that suits their stage and situation. Call Precision Dental on {{site:phone}} or book online.

faq.q: How do I know if a tooth is causing distress?
a: Watch for refusing food, chewing on one side, pulling at the face, new agitation at mealtimes, disturbed sleep or bad breath. Pain is a common and overlooked cause of distressed behaviour.

faq.q: What if they will not let me brush their teeth?
a: Try a different time of day, stand beside rather than in front, use the hand-over-hand method, and accept once daily if twice is not achievable. Forcing it rarely works.
Where possible, yes. Completing necessary work while the person can tolerate and consent to it makes later maintenance much easier.

faq.q: Can you see someone with dementia at the practice?
a: Yes. We allow longer appointments, schedule for the time of day they are usually at their best, and welcome a familiar carer to stay throughout.

faq.q: What about dentures in residential care?
a: Have them clearly labelled with a name, cleaned daily and removed overnight. Ask the facility about its oral care policy and who assists.
